rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address shifts from singular, addressing the Prophet, to plural, addressing humanity in general.
rows.anchor: These verses transition from the second-person singular, in which the Prophet is addressed, to the second-person plural, addressing humanity in general.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording closely parallels 76:27.
rows.anchor: An almost identical verse is 76:27; see 76:27c.

rows.speaker: some other schools of recitation
rows.claim: Some recitation schools read the verbs in the third person plural: they love the ephemeral and forsake the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: According to some other schools of recitation, they can be read in the third person plural

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kallā is emphatic and negative here as “Nay,” but may also be read affirmatively as “truly” or “indeed.”
rows.anchor: Nay translates the emphatic particle kallā, which can also be read in the affirmative, meaning “truly” or “indeed.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reaching of the collarbones refers to the soul's moment of death, as it is about to leave the body.
rows.anchor: It refers to the soul, and its reaching the collarbones refers to the moment of death when the soul is about to leave the body

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: IK says the negative reading means death discloses truth beyond denial, while the affirmative reading means the soul's departure is certain.
rows.anchor: When kallā is read in the affirmative, the verse indicates there is no doubt that the soul will leave the body (IK).

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: JJ takes aimless to mean being left without revealed religious obligations or accountability.
rows.anchor: without being obligated to follow a revealed religion and without being held accountable?” (JJ).

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: IK also understands aimless as neglected, referring to people who doubt that they will be resurrected.
rows.anchor: Left aimless could also be understood to mean“neglected,” in which case it refers to those who doubt they will be resurrected (IK).

rows.speaker: JJ, Ṭs
rows.claim: JJ and Ṭs understand the verse to describe revelation in periodic installments rather than the Quran descending all at once.
rows.anchor: God revealed the Quran, that is, in periodic installments rather than all at once (JJ, Ṭs).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's creation of the sky, which some opponents already accepted, is evidence that He can resurrect people as He wills; the verse links this argument to 40:57 and 36:81.
rows.anchor: is here cited as evidence that God would have no problem resurrecting human beings as He wills

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky, its night and day, and the spread earth are further dimensions of creation demonstrating God's power to create and resurrect.
rows.anchor: These verses describe additional dimensions of creation, which demonstrate that God can create and resurrect as He will.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky's canopy refers to its highest level.
rows.anchor: Its canopy indicates the highest level of the sky

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fashioning the sky means making it whole, without fissures, cracks, or imperfections; its perfection is linked to 67:3–4.
rows.anchor: fashioned it implies that it is whole with no fissures, cracks, or imperfections

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍuḥāhā, rendered “its day,” can also mean its light, morning brightness, or morning; compare 93:1 and 79:46.
rows.anchor: Its day translates ḍuḥāhā, which could also mean “its light,” “its morning brightness,”as in 93:1, or the morning, as in v. 46.

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The earth's mention after the sky, night, and day indicates that it was created after the heavens had been established.
rows.anchor: of the earth (v. 30) after the sky, night, and day indicates that the earth was created after the heavens had been established (Q).

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some take the pastures as an allusion to all plant life.
rows.anchor: Its pastures is interpreted by some as an allusion to all plant life

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others understand the pastures as everything eaten by human beings and animals.
rows.anchor: and by others as an allusion to everything eaten by human beings and animals.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sustains all things and makes them serve human beings, including by providing sustenance for people and their flocks.
rows.anchor: God sustains all things and has made all things subservient to human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As God's vicegerents, humans should thank Him for sustenance and share these resources with all creatures.
rows.anchor: Human beings are thus God’s vicegerents (see, e.g., 2:30; 6:165c; 35:39)

rows.speaker: IK, Q
rows.claim: One interpretation is that God made birth easy, so the baby can come forth from the mother's womb.
rows.anchor: From one perspective, this verse refers to the ease with which a baby comes forth from the mother’s womb (IK, Q)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that God made the way easy by providing all people with guidance, as 76:3 says.
rows.anchor: it refers to God’s providing all people with guidance, as in 76:3: Truly We guided him upon the way, be he grateful or ungrateful (IK).

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: A further interpretation is that God makes it easy for each thing to perform the function for which it was created.
rows.anchor: Some interpret it as an indication that God has made it easy for everything to perform the function

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source cites a famous hadith saying that each person’s created function has been made easy for them.
rows.anchor: in a famous ḥadīth, “Work, for that for which each person was created has been made easy for him”

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: One view takes food as a sign for reflection that helps people appreciate God's power and mercy.
rows.anchor: signs upon which human beings should reflect in order to appreciate fully God’s Power and Mercy (Q)

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Another view links reflection on eating and elimination to what becomes of the world.
rows.anchor: Others say that it relates to reflecting upon the consumption and elimination of food, for that is an example of what becomes of the world (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Vegetation emerges through fissures that split the earth; related descriptions of vegetation and the earth revived by water occur at 6:99, 29:63, 30:24, 31:10, 35:27, and 39:21.
rows.anchor: Vegetation comes through the fissures, splitting the earth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The provisions of the natural world invite reflection that deepens understanding of God's wisdom; creation is true, all creation glorifies God, and creation connects with revelation. The passage echoes 79:33.
rows.anchor: These verses reflect the continuous Quranic emphasis on the benefits that God has provided through the natural world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spread pages are the opening of the record of deeds; at Judgment people review an exhaustive account, as in 18:49, and no deed is hidden. Related passages describe the record books and their contents.
rows.anchor: When the pages are spread refers to the opening of the book in which people’s deeds are recorded.
